situation: You are a developer on a data team. Your manager, Laura, asked you to deliver a dashboard by Friday, but a data source you depend on is still broken. You need more time.
tasks: Explain why you cannot finish the dashboard by Friday.
Ask for a specific new deadline and say what you can deliver on Friday.
Offer one way to reduce the risk of further delays.

situation: You just had a 45-minute meeting with two colleagues from the regulatory team about a new reporting tool. Several decisions were made, but nothing is written down yet.
tasks: Thank everyone for their time and summarize the two main decisions.
List who is responsible for each next step and the date.
Ask the team to reply if you missed or misunderstood anything.

situation: A senior colleague, Mark, invited you to join a side project that would take about five hours a week. You are already close to your limit with your current tasks.
tasks: Thank Mark and show that you value the invitation.
Decline politely and explain your reason without sounding negative.
Suggest an alternative, such as joining later or recommending someone else.

situation: Your team uses a cloud analytics platform from an outside vendor. Since last Tuesday, exported reports have contained duplicate rows, and this is affecting your weekly numbers.
tasks: Describe the bug clearly, including when it started and what you expected to happen.
Explain the impact on your team and how urgent the problem is.
Ask for a status update and offer logs or screenshots to help them investigate.

situation: A new teammate, Priya, is starting on Monday. You will be her onboarding buddy for the first two weeks.
tasks: Welcome Priya and say what her first day will look like.
Tell her which tools and accounts she should expect to receive access to.
Invite her to ask questions and suggest a short call on Monday morning.

situation: Your manager scheduled a team meeting at the same time as a client workshop you must attend. You cannot be in both places.
tasks: Explain the scheduling conflict politely.
Propose a solution, such as joining for part of the meeting or sending written updates.
Ask whether someone could share the notes with you afterward.

situation: Two weeks ago you sent a proposal for a new internal tool to a director, Elena Ruiz. You have not received any reply, and the budget discussion is next week.
tasks: Politely follow up and remind her what the proposal is about.
Explain why a decision before next week would help.
Offer to present the main points in a short meeting.

situation: You discovered that a model you built produced wrong numbers in last month's report because of a data-cleaning mistake of your own. The report has already been shared with several stakeholders.
tasks: Take responsibility for the mistake without making excuses.
Explain what went wrong, what the correct figures are, and how big the difference is.
Describe the concrete steps you will take to prevent this from happening again.

situation: You would like to attend a three-day online conference about machine learning in healthcare. It costs 400 dollars and takes place during working hours.
tasks: Ask your manager for permission to attend and for the budget.
Explain two ways the conference would benefit your work.
Explain how you will cover your tasks while you are away.

situation: A colleague from another department keeps sending you urgent requests at the last minute. This week alone you received three, and it is hurting your own planned work.
tasks: Acknowledge that her projects matter and keep a professional, friendly tone.
Describe the problem and its effect on your work with specific examples.
Propose a clear process, such as a request form or a weekly check-in, and ask for her opinion.

situation: You gave a presentation to a group of non-technical managers yesterday. One of them, David, asked a detailed question about data privacy that you could not answer on the spot.
tasks: Thank David for the question and admit that you did not have a full answer.
Give a clear answer or explain how you will find one.
Offer to meet or send documentation so he feels confident about the topic.

situation: You need to ask an outside consultant, Dr. Hall, for access to a sample dataset she mentioned in a webinar. You have never spoken to her before.
tasks: Introduce yourself and explain how you found her work.
Describe what you want to do with the dataset and why it is useful.
Ask about any conditions for using it and suggest a call if that is easier.

situation: You are leaving your current project in two weeks to join another team. Your teammate Sam will take over your responsibilities, and he is nervous about the handover.
tasks: Reassure Sam and describe the handover plan in general terms.
List the most important tasks, risks and contacts he needs to know about.
Schedule time for questions and explain how he can reach you after you leave.

situation: You were sick for three days and missed an important deadline for sending a status report to your project manager, Ana.
tasks: Apologize briefly and explain what happened.
Say when you will send the report.
Ask Ana if there is anything else you should prioritize this week.

situation: Your team lead asked everyone for feedback on a new policy that requires three office days per week. You work well remotely and your team is spread across two time zones.
tasks: State your position on the policy respectfully and clearly.
Give two reasons, using concrete examples from your own work or your team's results.
Suggest a compromise and offer to help test it for a month.

professor: Dr. Rivera: This week we are discussing artificial intelligence in the workplace. Some people believe AI tools will make most employees more productive, while others worry they will reduce the number of available jobs. What is your view? Explain your position and support it with reasons or examples.
studentA: Maya: I think AI will mainly help workers. When I use a coding assistant, I finish boring tasks faster and I can spend more time on design and problem solving. New technologies usually create new kinds of jobs too.
studentB: Tomas: I am more worried. Companies want to save money, and if one person can do the work of three with AI, they may not hire the other two. Workers need protection and training, not just optimism.

professor: Prof. Chen: Many universities now allow students to use AI chatbots for homework and essays, as long as they say so. Do you think this is a good policy? Share your opinion and explain how education should respond to these tools.
studentA: Lucia: I agree with the policy. Banning AI is unrealistic, and students will use it anyway. It is better to teach them to check the answers and to think critically about what the tool produces.
studentB: Ben: I disagree. If a chatbot writes the essay, the student does not practice writing or thinking. Schools should focus more on oral exams and in-class writing, where students cannot rely on the tool.

professor: Dr. Okafor: Remote work has become common in many industries. Do you think working from home is better than working in an office? Give your opinion and explain what you think is the biggest advantage or disadvantage.
studentA: Sara: I prefer working from home. I save two hours of commuting every day, and I can concentrate better without interruptions. My productivity has clearly improved.
studentB: Jake: I like the office more. I learn faster when I can ask a colleague a quick question, and working at home makes it hard for me to separate work from personal life.

professor: Prof. Alvarez: Social media companies collect large amounts of data about their users in order to show personalized content and ads. Is this an acceptable trade-off for free services? Discuss and give reasons for your view.
studentA: Nina: I think it is acceptable if users clearly understand what is collected. Nobody pays for the service, so the data is the price. The real problem is that most people never read the terms.
studentB: Omar: I do not think it is a fair trade. Companies know far more about us than we know about them, and personalized feeds can manipulate people. Governments should limit what can be collected.

professor: Dr. Patel: Some schools have introduced a four-day school week to improve student well-being and save money. Do you think this is a good idea? Explain your position and consider how it could affect students and families.
studentA: Chloe: It sounds like a good idea to me. Students would have more time to rest and to follow their interests, and teachers would be less stressed, which improves lessons.
studentB: Ryan: I see a problem for families. Many parents work five days, so they would need to find childcare. Also, longer school days could make children too tired to learn well.

professor: Prof. Lindqvist: Video games are often criticized for being a waste of time or for causing addiction. At the same time, researchers study their benefits for learning, teamwork and mental health. To what extent do you think games have a positive effect on society?
studentA: Elena: Games can teach cooperation and problem solving, and online communities give lonely people a place to belong. The risk is mainly excessive use, which is a design problem, not a problem with games themselves.
studentB: Marcus: I accept some benefits, but many games use mechanics intentionally designed to keep players hooked. We should be careful about praising games without regulating loot boxes and similar systems.

professor: Dr. Brooks: Learning a second language is often described as an important skill for the future. Do you think everyone should learn English, or is it better to focus on other skills? Give your opinion with examples.
studentA: Ana: I think English is essential for science, technology and business. Most resources I use for my studies are in English, so learning it opened many doors for me.
studentB: Leo: English is useful, but not everybody needs it. Someone who works locally could benefit more from practical skills. Also, translation tools are improving quickly.

professor: Prof. Nakamura: Companies increasingly use algorithms to screen job applications. Supporters say this is more objective than human recruiters, while critics say algorithms can repeat existing biases. Where do you stand, and what safeguards, if any, would you require?
studentA: Julia: Algorithms are consistent, which human recruiters are not. If we audit them regularly, they can be fairer than a tired person reading hundreds of resumes.
studentB: Daniel: The problem is that they learn from historical hiring data, which often contains bias. Without transparency, candidates cannot even understand why they were rejected.

professor: Dr. Flores: Many cities are trying to reduce car traffic by building bike lanes and improving public transport. Should governments restrict private cars in city centers? Explain your opinion and think about the costs and benefits.
studentA: Hannah: Yes, I support restrictions. Cities with fewer cars have cleaner air and safer streets, and people actually spend more time in local shops once the streets are pleasant.
studentB: Victor: It depends on the city. If public transport is unreliable, people simply have no choice. Restrictions without good alternatives would punish workers who live far from the center.

professor: Prof. Murphy: Open-source software is built and maintained by communities, often without payment. Should large companies that benefit from open-source projects be required to financially support them? Discuss your view.
studentA: Isabel: I think companies should pay. They earn millions using free tools, while the maintainers burn out. Funding would make important projects more secure and sustainable.
studentB: Kevin: A requirement would go against the idea of open source, which is that anyone can use the code freely. Voluntary sponsorship is better, and companies can also contribute developer time.

professor: Dr. Santos: Many people say that mental health should be taught in schools just like math or science. Do you agree? Explain why or why not, and say what students could learn.
studentA: Paula: I agree completely. Many teenagers feel stress and anxiety but do not know how to talk about it. Learning basic skills, like managing emotions, would help them for life.
studentB: Greg: It is a good idea, but teachers are not therapists. Schools need trained professionals, otherwise the classes could become superficial or even cause problems.

professor: Prof. Weber: Some startups promote a culture of working extremely long hours, claiming it is necessary for success. Others argue that sustainable work habits produce better results. Which approach do you find more convincing, and why?
studentA: Camila: In the early stages, intense effort may be unavoidable, but it cannot last. People who are exhausted make poor decisions, and the best employees leave when burnout begins.
studentB: Ian: Founders often say this culture is a choice, but it favors people without family responsibilities. A company that depends on overwork has a weak business model, not strong commitment.

professor: Dr. Kim: Online communities, such as Discord servers, have become important places where young people make friends and share interests. Do you think these communities are good for social development? Give reasons for your opinion.
studentA: Rosa: They are very good, especially for shy people. I met friends who share my interests, and I can practice communicating without feeling as much pressure as in person.
studentB: Tyler: I think they are useful but incomplete. Online friendships can feel intense, yet they are easier to leave, and some servers have toxic or unsafe behavior without enough moderation.

professor: Prof. Dubois: Self-driving cars could greatly reduce accidents, but they will also face situations in which any decision causes harm. Who should be responsible when an autonomous vehicle causes an accident: the manufacturer, the owner or the software developer? Defend your position.
studentA: Alicia: The manufacturer should be responsible, because it designs and sells the whole system. Owners cannot control decisions made by software they do not understand.
studentB: Peter: I think responsibility should be shared. Owners must maintain the vehicle and update software, and regulators should define clear standards, otherwise companies could avoid accountability.

professor: Dr. Haddad: Some people believe that university education is necessary for a good career, while others say that learning skills online or through work experience is enough. What is your opinion? Include an example from your own life or from someone you know.
studentA: Mia: I think a degree still matters. It gives you a structured education and opens doors, especially in fields like medicine or engineering where employers ask for it.
studentB: Sam: In software, my friends who learned on their own got good jobs because they built real projects. Experience can be more valuable than a certificate, and it costs much less.
